title: Remove Duplicates From an Unsorted Linked List
statement:
`head` is the first node of a singly linked list whose values are in no particular order. Call a value *repeated* when two or more nodes of the list carry it. Delete every node holding a repeated value (all of its copies, not only the extras) and leave the remaining nodes in their original order.

Return the head of the list that remains. It may be empty, in which case return an empty list.
notes:
## Intuition

Whether a node survives depends on the whole list: a value that looks unique now may show up again near the tail. A brute-force idea compares each value with every other node, which is O(n²). Instead, count every value in one pass first. After that, each node can be judged on the spot, and a second pass unlinks the nodes whose value has a count above 1.

## Approach

1. Walk the list once and store how many times each value occurs in the map `count`.
2. Put a `dummy` node in front of `head`, so deleting the first node needs no special case. `prev` starts at `dummy`.
3. While `prev.next` exists, look at its value. If `count` says it occurs more than once, bypass that node by setting `prev.next = prev.next.next` and keep `prev` where it is.
4. Otherwise the node stays, so move `prev` onto it.
5. Return `dummy.next`.

## Example 1, step by step

List `1 → 2 → 3 → 2`. The first pass gives `count = {1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 1}`.

- `prev = dummy`, next value `1` occurs once: `prev` moves to `1`.
- Next value `2` occurs twice: `1.next` now skips to `3`.
- Next value `3` occurs once: `prev` moves to `3`.
- Next value `2` occurs twice: `3.next` becomes `null`, and the loop ends.

The result is `[1, 3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): two passes over the list, each with O(1) map work per node.
- Space: O(k) for the map, where k is the number of distinct values.

## Pitfalls

- Keeping the first copy of each value solves a different problem; every copy of a repeated value must go.
- After unlinking a node, do not advance `prev`: the new `prev.next` has not been checked yet.
- A single pass that deletes "values seen before" misses the first copy; the counts must be complete first.
- The answer can be empty (`[2, 1, 1, 2]`), which the dummy node handles naturally.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | map from each value to how many nodes hold it |
| `node` | cursor for the counting pass |
| `dummy` | placeholder node in front of `head` |
| `prev` | last node known to stay; its successor is the one being judged |
